learningObjective: Explain the motivation for gradient bucketing in data-parallel training and the trade-off it induces.

canonicalClaims.claim: Gradient bucketing groups multiple small gradient tensors into a single larger AllReduce payload to amortize the per-collective latency term (α) and better saturate link bandwidth, at the cost of delaying the launch of the collective until all tensors in the bucket are ready.
conditions: The collective cost is well modelled as α + βS with a non-negligible α (latency).
The per-layer gradients are small enough that many of them fall inside the latency-dominated regime.
Bucket boundaries respect backward-order availability so the bucket can be dispatched as early as possible.
nonImplications: Does not imply that larger buckets are always better: a bucket that spans too many layers delays overlap with backward compute.
Does not imply that bucketing changes numerical results (aside from reduction ordering effects).

misconceptions.claim: Bucketing exists because NCCL requires all AllReduces to be issued in a single call per iteration.
misconceptions.whyWrong: NCCL supports many AllReduces per iteration; bucketing is a policy for grouping payloads, not a NCCL requirement.

misconceptions.claim: Bucketing improves accuracy by summing more gradients before averaging, reducing variance in the AllReduce operator.
misconceptions.whyWrong: AllReduce is exact (up to FP ordering); bucketing is a performance optimization and does not change the reduced value beyond floating-point ordering effects.

misconceptions.claim: Bucket size should always be chosen as small as possible so that each layer's AllReduce can start immediately when its gradient is ready.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Very small buckets pay the latency α for each launch, wasting bandwidth. A balance between bandwidth utilization and overlap window is needed.
